issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used specifically as a distraction is not impossible, but in this profile it stands out as poorly integrated with the rest of the selected items. The rest of the presentation centers on assault-related fear, hypervigilance, restricted safety, intrusive memories, and alcohol/drug use or mental rehearsal as coping. Physical self-harm introduces a qualitatively different coping pattern that is not supported elsewhere in the triggers, threat, appraisal, or memory items, making the strategy set less coherent.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Lost my connection to my community and culture' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and demographics as presented. The other appraisal items are highly individual and interpersonal ('can't rely on myself', 'permanently an outsider now'), but this item specifically implies a cultural/community rupture that is not otherwise reflected in the triggers, threat items, or other appraisals. Given the provided demographic context, it reads as insufficiently grounded rather than clearly linked to the rest of this sexual-assault formulation.

vignette:
Martha is a sixty-nine-year-old agricultural worker who has been married for over forty years. She came to therapy reluctantly, at the urging of her daughter, after her PCL-5 score of 67 indicated severe posttraumatic symptoms. For decades, Martha had managed to keep the assault locked away, but in the past year, it had begun leaking through the cracks of her carefully constructed life.

The assault happened when Martha was twenty-two, working the early shift at a produce packing plant. She had stayed late to clean a conveyor belt, and a supervisor she had trusted cornered her in the back storage room. She still remembered the smell of diesel and rotting onions, the feel of concrete against her cheek, the way his belt buckle pressed into her lower back. She told no one. She went home, showered, and went to work the next day. She had come to believe, in the years that followed, that she should have been able to stop it—that she should have seen it coming, should have fought harder, should have been a different kind of woman. That belief had calcified into something harder: she could not rely on herself. If she could not protect herself from a man she knew, in a building she worked in every day, then she could not trust her own judgment about anything.

The memory did not stay buried. It came to her suddenly, without warning, usually when she was least prepared—while washing dishes, or in the middle of the night, or, most troublingly, on the bus. Public transport had become a nightmare. Every time a man sat too close, every time the bus lurched and someone’s arm brushed against hers, the memory surged back with full sensory force. She had stopped riding the bus unless absolutely necessary. Her husband drove her to the fields now, but that meant she had to coordinate her shifts around his schedule, and sometimes she was late. Her supervisor had noticed. Martha had started making excuses.

Certain conversation topics could trigger her as well. When other women in the packing shed talked about their husbands, or when someone mentioned a late shift, or when a male coworker made a joke she could not quite hear, Martha’s stomach would drop. She had learned to keep her head down, to move away, to pretend she had not heard. She had become an expert at disappearing in plain sight. But the cost was loneliness. She felt, with a certainty that had only grown stronger over the decades, that she was permanently an outsider now—set apart from other people by something they could not see and she could not explain. She was certain that if anyone knew what had happened, they would see her differently, so she kept everyone at a distance.

To manage the constant dread, Martha had developed habits that made sense to her but had slowly shrunk her world. She checked behind her constantly—when walking to the car, when entering a room, when standing at the sink. She only felt safe in a very limited number of places: her own kitchen, the back corner of the packing shed where she had a clear view of the door, her daughter’s living room if her son-in-law was not home. Anywhere else, she was on high alert, scanning for exits, for faces, for anything that felt wrong. She drank most evenings—just enough wine to take the edge off, she told herself—and she had begun rehearsing worst-case scenarios in her head before any outing, running through what she would do if a man approached, if the bus broke down, if someone cornered her again. It was exhausting, but it felt like the only way to stay safe.

What finally brought Martha to therapy was not the fear itself, but the isolation. Her husband had grown frustrated with her refusals to attend family gatherings, her daughter had cried on the phone, and Martha had realized she could not remember the last time she had felt truly at ease in another person’s company. She was afraid of what therapy might uncover—afraid that talking about it would make the memories worse, afraid that she would be judged, afraid that she was too old to change. But she was also, beneath the fear, hoping for something she could barely name: a way to feel less alone in her own life.
